newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechnya, Russia hope for breakthrough agreement.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya, Russia hope for breakthrough agreement.

text.p: Russian and Chechen officials reported progress at talks on their future relations on Sunday and said they hoped to sign an agreement in the next eight days to end confrontation between them.

"Centuries-old confrontation, of which there have been relapses every now and then, is coming to an end," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Russian negotiator Ivan Rybkin as telling a news conference in the Chechen capital Grozny.

But there was no indication that either side had altered its stance in the dispute over Chechnya's demands for independence which caused a nearly 21-month conflict that killed tens of thousands of people before it ended last August.
Moscow, anxious not to encourage other separatist-minded Russian regions, has ruled out secession and deferred a decision on Chechnya's political status until the year 2001.
The mainly Moslem region's leaders openly defy Moscow, saying they are already independent.

Completion of a political agreement, or a series of agreements on economic issues, should help increase trust between the two sides and signal their mutual determination to wor out a way to live together in peace.
Rybkin, secretary of the Security Council which includes Russia's top leaders, indicated earlier on Sunday that the political document would amount to a formal peace declaration.
He said the signing of the agreement would depend on President Boris Yeltsin's working schedule but hoped it could be completed in the first 10 days of this month.
Rybkin said the two sides had also reached draft agreements on social and economic issues and money circulation.
Interfax news agency quoted him as saying Chechnya would "work in the rouble zone and an agreement to this effect has already been worked out", but gave no details.
Top Chechen negotiator Movladi Udogov also emerged confident from Sunday's talks, describing them as "fruitful".

"We did considerable work on the documents which are practically ready for signing," said Udugov. "Today we can avoid sharp movements and sign documents which would put an end to confrontation in the Caucasus."
He said the political agreement would reflect the needs of both Moscow and Chechnya but gave no details.
Russia is trying to persuade Chechnya that it would be economically advantageous to remain part of Russia.
Much of the small region, an oil-refining centre, is in ruins and Chechnya needs Russian money to help rebuild its shattered infrastructure.

Russian troops, sent to Chechnya in December 1994, have pulled out but the guerrillas who fought them still have many of their weapons and Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov faces a difficult task trying to maintain order.
An Italian photographer, Mauro Galligani, was still missing on Sunday a week after he was seized by four armed and masked men outside Grozny.
